newsitem.title: USA: Pena wants plan to cut dependence on oil imports.
newsitem.headline: Pena wants plan to cut dependence on oil imports.

text.p: The United States needs a programme with timetables and targets to reduce dependence on imported energy that is reaching an "unacceptable" level, President Clinton's choice for Energy secretary, Federico Pena, said Thursday.

"I believe that we will not reverse our slide toward energy insecurity without a set of strategies that address both energy production and consumption and that are coupled with specific targets and timetables to measure performance," Pena said at his confirmation hearing before the Senate Energy Committee.
He said by 2010 the country will rely on imports to meet 60 percent of its oil needs, and that 70 percent of the world's oil exports will be from the Mideast Gulf. "This is unacceptable," he said.
Without goals and deadlines, he said, "I'm concerned we're going to fall further and further behind."

Also at the hearing, where he received a generally favourable reception, Pena fended off calls from some senators to build a temporary dump for nuclear wastes accumulating at commercial reactors and other sites until a permanent storage facility is built.

Pena, Transportation secretary in Clinton's first term, said the administration has made progress in determining whether Yucca Mountain in Nevada will be a suitable place to stash nuclear waste permanently, and said he would make every effort to see that a decision can be made next year.

Pena acknowledged that by next January the federal government will be in violation of a law that requires it to start taking spent fuel from commercial reactors. He said he planned to have the department get to work immediately to determine the amount of liability the government would face because of this.
Committee Chairman Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, said potential liability is "so astronomical that we can't even get an estimate."

Forty-six state agencies and 33 utilities, meanwhile, filed another lawsuit Thursday against the Energy Department over the nuclear waste issue, and asked a federal court to approve their stopping payments into a federal fund to build a dump.

Clinton last year threatened to veto a bill pushed by Murkowski and supported by 63 senators that would put a temporary dump near Yucca. Clinton said the bill, opposed by Nevada lawmakers, would prejudge Yucca as the permanent site.
While some senators criticised the Clinton administration's policies on nuclear waste and energy security, most committee sources said they expected the panel to approve Pena's nomination.
"I am not uncomfortable with the fact that you do not have a long background in the energy field. In fact, I think that might be an advantage," Sen. Slade Gorton, a Washington Republican, said.
Pena was a late selection for Energy secretary, and critics have questioned whether he has sufficient background in energy issues.

"The critics have said your nomination is evidence the White House doesn't care about the department, that it was a 'throw away' position and a 'white flag' has gone up" over the building that houses the department, Murkowski said.
A number of Republicans have called for dismantling the Energy Department and farming its operations out to other agencies, a move the administration opposes.
